name: Bhagat Singh
summary: Bhagat Singh sought Indian independence from British rule and a socialist transformation led by workers and peasants. He argued for universal adult suffrage, opposed communal politics and caste exclusion, and saw international solidarity as part of the struggle against exploitation.

all-land-state-owned.rationale: The programme calls for nationalization of land by the revolutionary state.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: He argued that social and economic conditions gave rise to revolutionary opportunities and that isolated armed acts could be harmful without organized mass support.

armed-resistance-to-occupation.rationale: The tribunal found that Singh participated in armed action to overthrow British rule in India.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: Our Opportunity describes the breakdown of the capitalist order as inevitable despite short-term measures that might postpone it.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: He argued that avoiding imperial wars required ending capitalist exploitation and expected war to disappear after a socialist transition.

class-collaboration.rationale: He urged peasants and workers to organize independently against their own exploiters and argued that the Congress leadership protected the interests of Indian capitalists.

clerical-rule.rationale: In his essays on communal riots and religion in the independence struggle he opposed giving religious authority a role in politics and defended common civil rights.

collective-farming.rationale: He gave the transition to collective farming as the purpose of nationalizing agricultural land.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: He denounced the exploitation of Indian labour under British rule and made ending imperial exploitation a goal of the revolutionary programme.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: He called for proletarian dictatorship to clear the way for the revolutionary social order and treated it as a transitional stage in his introduction to Dreamland.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: He denied the existence of a supreme being and argued that theories of divine justice help excuse the power of privileged groups.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: In The Issue of Untouchability he demanded equal rights and actual access to schools, wells and roads for people excluded on caste grounds. His essay on communal riots called for an end to discrimination by religion, colour, race and nationality.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: He condemned a system in which the people producing goods went without necessities while the class that appropriated their labour accumulated wealth.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: He argued that transferring office from British officials to Indian elites would do little for workers and peasants without a socialist transformation.

informal-organisation.rationale: He called for a durable, disciplined party of full-time organizers with regular meetings, conferences and training.

labour-priority-over-capital.rationale: He called labour the foundation of society and demanded political sovereignty for the workers whose output was appropriated by capitalists.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Religion and Our Freedom Struggle rejects scriptural authority as a basis for settling disputes over citizens’ rights and treats religious philosophy as a matter of personal opinion.

martyrs-honoured.rationale: In Youth and his profiles of Indian revolutionaries he celebrated those who died in the struggle against British rule and urged readers to remember their sacrifices.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: In The Religious Riots and Their Solution he treated material needs as the underlying cause of social action. He also argued that revolutions arise from prevailing social and economic conditions.

more-religion-public.rationale: He assigned religious belief to personal life and blamed its intrusion into common politics for deepening communal divisions.

national-church-status.rationale: In his essay on communal riots he treated religion as a private concern and explicitly endorsed separating it from politics.

night-watchman-state.rationale: He proposed that a revolutionary government use its resources for mass education and for the constructive work of building a socialist society.

no-denominational-politics.rationale: In The Religious Riots and Their Solution he argued that people of different faiths could organize together politically once religion was kept out of politics.

no-transition-to-communism.rationale: He distinguished the taking of power and the transitional revolutionary government from the later construction of a socialist society.

opposition-only-legal-channels.rationale: The tribunal documented Singh’s participation in a campaign that used illegal force against British colonial authority.

parliamentary-road-socialism.rationale: He considered legislative activity useful for organizing and winning concessions, and argued that a revolutionary transfer of power had to precede socialist reconstruction.

patriotism-serves-workers.rationale: He challenged appeals to national sentiment without concrete benefits for peasants and workers and made their emancipation the goal of his independence struggle.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: He made world federation an objective of his revolutionary programme and praised it again in his introduction to Dreamland.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: He argued that literary inheritance matters to national progress and wanted Indians to be able to read their classical literature and develop their own languages.

profit-exploitation.rationale: He argued that the owners and exploiters who accumulated wealth did so by taking the fruits of workers’ labour.

property-franchise.rationale: He expressly called for abolishing property qualifications and introducing universal adult voting.

property-fundamental.rationale: He proposed ending landlordism and transferring land and industries to public ownership.

public-ownership.rationale: The economic programme calls for the nationalization of industry as part of industrializing India.

racial-franchise.rationale: He called for the vote for every adult and for the elimination of discrimination by race and nationality.

reason-over-faith.rationale: He treated independent criticism and reasoning as essential and argued that beliefs must withstand rational scrutiny.

rehabilitation.rationale: He endorsed the reformative theory of punishment and argued that prisons should be designed to reclaim offenders.

religion-illusion.rationale: He interpreted belief in a protective God as a human response to helplessness and misery and described prayer as a consolation for distress.

religions-one-truth.rationale: He treated the religions’ conflicting claims as human attempts to explain a world they did not yet understand and rejected their supernatural explanations.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: In Religion and Our Freedom Struggle he called for competing religious philosophies to have the standing of personal opinions and gave civil rights priority in public disputes.

religious-nation.rationale: In The Religious Riots and Their Solution he praised young Indians for identifying as citizens of one country across Hindu, Muslim and Sikh affiliations.

scripture-inerrant.rationale: He rejected divine authorship as an authority for belief and criticized treating the Veda or Quran as unquestionable truth in Religion and Our Freedom Struggle.

separate-church-state.rationale: In The Religious Riots and Their Solution he endorsed keeping religion personal and separating it from politics.

smash-state-machine.rationale: He defined revolution as the reconstruction of society on a new basis after the complete destruction of the existing regime.

socialism-needs-workers-power.rationale: He set proletarian sovereignty as an explicit goal in his court statement and described the socialist revolution as a revolution by and for workers.

state-class-instrument.rationale: He described government machinery as the ruling class’s instrument for safeguarding and advancing its own interests.

state-harmful.rationale: His mature Marxist programme called for a revolutionary government to take power and reconstruct society. His earlier What Is Anarchism? discusses abolition of the state as the anarchists’ position.

strong-leader.rationale: He criticized the Viceroy for overriding legislative decisions and denounced the proposal for provincial governors with extraordinary powers over elected bodies.

territorial-expansion.rationale: He rejected imperialist war aims and war trophies in his account of a future revolutionary society.

unions-good.rationale: In The Religious Riots and Their Solution he credited trade-union organization with helping workers resist communal violence. He also called for revolutionary organizers to build labour unions.

vanguard-party.rationale: His programme called for a disciplined party of full-time revolutionaries to organize workers and peasants and lead the transition to socialism.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: In Students and Politics he argued that students had a duty to understand and participate in politics while pursuing their studies.

women-suffrage.rationale: He demanded the vote for every adult and expressly included women on the same terms as men.

worker-farmer-alliance.rationale: He identified peasants and industrial workers as the social forces that needed to organize together to carry out the revolution.

workers-anti-imperialist-capitalist-alli.rationale: He argued that the anticolonial movement could not rely on capitalists who feared risking their property, and called for workers and peasants to organize around their own interests.

workers-nation.rationale: His essay on communal riots put common class interests above religious and national divisions, and his Assembly statement made international worker solidarity central to his proposed world federation.

workers-own-party.rationale: He called for a communist party with its own programme and for organizing worker and peasant political bodies beyond the Congress leadership.

workers-parties-campaign-reforms.rationale: He advised revolutionaries to accept partial reforms as gains during the struggle and to keep organizing for their ultimate aims.

booksNotUsed.reason: The Jail Notebook mainly copies or summarizes other writers. These reading notes do not establish that Singh adopted each position he recorded.

notes: The audit uses Singh’s mature prison writings for his political programme. The 1923 language essay is used only for the position it describes. The Jail Notebook was checked as a collection of reading notes, and passages attributed to other authors were excluded. Shared organizational texts were used only when Singh was an identified speaker or writer. The collected essays, letters, judgment and selected political writings were checked for economic policy, government design, civil liberties, caste, religion, language, foreign relations, and political methods, as well as for positions on ecology and technology.
